output.brief: The rise in chilled write-offs is mostly a receiving problem at the DC, not a Haverlow problem. Haverlow's trailers recorded 1.9–3.6°C and product at 2.4–3.5°C at door-open, with no alarms. Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four in week 31, night pallets wait a median of about 3 h 52 min instead of 44 min on unrefrigerated docks at 15–17°C. Night write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9%, and the rate is the same for Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label. Day shift is flat. Chamber temperatures were fine. The warm receiving probes are therefore real, but they measure warming on the dock rather than the supplier's fault. Don't raise the chargeback or move volume; that would penalise the wrong party. Don't drop the night probe either, since that would hide the problem. Lead with restoring night receiving to six and setting a maximum dock-to-chamber time, tracked weekly from scan data. Separately, sample Corriebank's claims against lots to see how much of the credit increase is over-claiming. That is unproven, so don't change their terms yet. I'm fairly confident in the main finding; the Corriebank share is unknown.
